title: Ferrofluid was invented at NASA in 1963 to pull rocket fuel towards a pump in zero gravity

cover.alt: Black ferrofluid raised into rows of sharp spikes by a magnet placed beneath it.

body: Ferrofluid is a liquid that leaps into a hedgehog of spikes when a magnet comes near. It was developed in 1963 by NASA’s Steve Papell as a rocket fuel that a magnetic field could draw towards the pump when there is no gravity to help. The recipe is roughly **5% magnetic particles** (magnetite or another iron compound, 10 nanometres or smaller), 10% surfactant to stop them clumping and 85% carrier liquid, usually oil. The particles are so small that they are magnetised only while a field is applied and lose it the moment the magnet goes, which is why the liquid is called a superparamagnet rather than a ferromagnet. The spikes appear above a critical field strength: the peaks concentrate the field, which lowers the magnetic energy, while gravity and surface tension fight to keep the surface flat.

slides.heading: About 5 in 100 parts of a ferrofluid, by volume, are magnetic particles
slides.note: Roughly 5% magnetic solids, 10% surfactant and 85% carrier liquid

slides.question: How big are the magnetic particles in a ferrofluid, in nanometres?
slides.explanation: About 10 nanometres or less, a hundred-thousandth of a millimetre. Being this small is what makes them lose their magnetism as soon as the magnet is taken away.

steps.label: A vertical magnetic field is applied

left.label: Ferromagnet
left.text: A fridge magnet or a magnetised iron bar keeps its magnetism after the field that made it is gone.

right.label: Ferrofluid
right.text: Its nanoparticles line up only while a field is applied and relax the moment it is removed: a superparamagnet, not a ferromagnet.

slides.heading: Where ferrofluid works
items: Loudspeakers: cooling the voice coil since 1973
Hard drives: seals around spinning shafts
Medicine: proposed drug targeting and hyperthermia

events.text: Steve Papell develops it at NASA
A permanently magnetic version is reported

slides.question: Why does ferrofluid go limp as soon as the magnet is removed?
slides.explanation: Particles about 10 nm across cannot hold a stable magnetisation on their own; they line up only while an external field is present, so the fluid is superparamagnetic, not ferromagnetic.
